ipp_page_h1: Hospital Isolated Power Panels (IPP) — NFPA 99 Compliant Solutions Across Saudi Arabia
ipp_page_subhead: Life-critical power protection for operating rooms, ICUs & wet procedure locations
ipp_what_heading: What Is an Isolated Power Panel?
ipp_what_p1: An isolated power panel (IPP) is a hospital-grade electrical system required in operating rooms and other "wet procedure locations" under NFPA 99. Instead of grounding the electrical system directly, an IPP electrically isolates the power supply so that a single ground fault does not trip the breaker or interrupt power — critical equipment stays running while the fault is detected and alarmed.
ipp_what_p2: This matters because in an operating room, an unexpected power interruption during a procedure is not just inconvenient — it can be dangerous. A line isolation monitor (LIM) continuously watches for faults and alerts staff immediately, giving the surgical team time to respond safely without the system cutting power outright.
ipp_step1_desc: Equipment sourcing matched to your facility's requirements, with compliance verification against NFPA 99 before anything is ordered.
ipp_step2_desc: Site assessment, electrical integration with existing systems, and equipotential grounding setup carried out by our installation team.
ipp_step3_desc: Full functional testing of every circuit and alarm, line isolation monitor calibration, and documentation before handover.
ipp_step4_desc: Hands-on training for hospital personnel on system operation, alarm response, and maintenance protocols.
ipp_step5_desc: Scheduled preventive maintenance, system inspections, and emergency response support to keep your IPP system compliant and reliable.

ups_what_p1: An Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) sits between the utility grid and your critical equipment, instantly switching to battery power the moment mains power fails or fluctuates outside safe limits. For mission-critical systems — servers, medical equipment, production lines, control rooms — even a fraction-of-a-second gap in power can mean lost data, halted processes, or equipment damage.
ups_what_p2: UPS systems range from small standby units protecting a single server rack to large online double-conversion systems supporting an entire data center or manufacturing floor. The right topology and capacity depend on your load profile, required runtime, and how much power quality protection your equipment needs beyond simple outage backup.

Unlike residential systems, commercial HVAC has to handle variable occupancy, mixed-use zones, and often continuous operation.
hvac_what_p2: Correct sizing matters more than most building owners realize — an oversized system short-cycles and wastes energy, while an undersized one never keeps up on peak summer days. We size systems against real load calculations for your building, not rule-of-thumb estimates, and integrate controls so the system runs efficiently rather than just running.

faq_a1: We serve clients nationwide across Saudi Arabia, with our strongest coverage in Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam, Al Khobar, and the Eastern Province. Site visits, installation, and maintenance are arranged based on your project location.

faq_q3: How do I request a quote?
faq_a3: You can request a quote through our contact page, by calling +966 560 224 715, or via WhatsApp. Include your project type and location so we can route your request to the right team.
faq_q4: Does Black Arrow only supply equipment, or do you also install and maintain it?
faq_a4: We handle the full lifecycle — supply, installation, testing/commissioning, and ongoing maintenance — for our core service lines (isolated power panels, EV charging, UPS, HVAC, lighting, firefighting, and electrical distribution).
faq_q5: What is an isolated power panel (IPP) and why do hospitals need one?
faq_a5: An isolated power panel is a hospital-grade electrical system required in operating rooms and other wet procedure locations under NFPA 99. It electrically isolates the power supply so a single ground fault doesn't interrupt power to life-critical equipment — a line isolation monitor alerts staff to the fault instead of cutting power outright.
faq_q6: Which IPP brands does Black Arrow supply?
faq_a6: We supply Bender isolated power panels (we are not an authorized or exclusive Bender dealer) and PG LifeLink IPP panels. Our designs are also compatible with Schneider Electric-style isolated power system specifications where a project calls for it.
faq_q7: What standards do your isolated power panels comply with?
faq_a7: Our IPP installations are engineered to NFPA 99, NFPA 70, and applicable SASO requirements for installed electrical equipment in Saudi Arabia.
faq_q8: What EV chargers does Black Arrow install?
faq_a8: We install AC Level 2 chargers (7–22kW) for workplaces and residential compounds, and DC fast chargers (50–350kW) for high-throughput commercial sites, with OCPP-compliant network management for multi-site operations and integrated POS/RFID payment where needed.
faq_q9: Can Black Arrow set up EV charging with a payment system?
faq_a9: Yes — we integrate POS, RFID card access, and mobile app payment options into commercial EV charging installations, along with OCPP-based remote monitoring and network management.
faq_q10: What size UPS system do I need?
faq_a10: It depends on your critical load and required runtime. We start with a load assessment to size the correct UPS capacity (we install systems from 1kVA up to 1MVA) and battery bank, rather than recommending a size before understanding your actual load profile.
faq_q11: What's the difference between online, line-interactive, and standby UPS?
faq_a11: Online (double-conversion) UPS continuously conditions power and offers the highest protection, suited to mission-critical loads. Line-interactive UPS regulates voltage and switches to battery on outage, a good middle-ground option. Standby UPS is the simplest and most economical, switching to battery only when mains power fails outright. We recommend the right topology based on your equipment's sensitivity and your budget.
faq_q12: Do you supply HVAC systems for both new buildings and retrofits?
faq_a12: Yes. We size systems based on a real load calculation for your building — whether it's new construction or a retrofit — rather than rule-of-thumb estimates, covering VRF/VRV systems, central chiller plants, and packaged rooftop units.
faq_q13: What fire suppression systems does Black Arrow install?
faq_a13: We install water sprinkler systems, clean-agent suppression (FM-200, CO₂), and water mist systems, matched to your facility's occupancy type and hazard classification, along with addressable fire alarm detection and hydrant/hose reel systems.
faq_q14: Are your fire safety systems compliant with Saudi civil defense requirements?
faq_a14: Yes, our fire detection and suppression designs follow NFPA 13 and NFPA 72 standards alongside Saudi Civil Defense requirements, with full testing and documentation provided for approval.
faq_q15: What electrical panel types does Black Arrow supply?
faq_a15: We supply and install main distribution boards (MDB), sub-distribution boards (SMDB), final distribution boards (DB), switchgear, and MCC/PLC/SCADA-integrated control panels for both low-voltage and medium-voltage systems.
faq_q16: What does a modular operating room (OR) project typically include?
faq_a16: A modular OR project typically includes design and layout planning, factory-prefabricated wall, ceiling, and service panels, on-site installation coordinated with your existing isolated power, medical gas, and HVAC systems, and testing/certification of air changes and pressure differentials before the room is released for clinical use.
faq_q21: How is lead shielding thickness determined for an X-ray or CT room?
faq_a21: Shielding thickness is calculated per room from the equipment's workload, use factor, occupancy factor of adjacent spaces, and distance — not a single standard number applied everywhere. We carry out the shielding survey and calculation before fabricating and installing the lead sheet, then verify the finished room with post-installation leakage testing.
faq_q17: How long does a typical installation project take?
faq_a17: Timelines vary by scope — a single UPS or EV charger installation can be completed in days, while a full electrical distribution upgrade or hospital IPP installation across multiple rooms takes longer. We provide a project timeline as part of every quote after a site assessment.
faq_q18: Do you offer maintenance contracts after installation?
faq_a18: Yes, we offer scheduled preventive maintenance for all our core service lines — including battery testing for UPS systems, filter/coil maintenance for HVAC, and periodic inspection and testing for fire safety and electrical distribution systems.

nfpa_post_h1: NFPA 99 Compliance for Saudi Hospitals: A Practical Guide
nfpa_post_subhead: What the standard covers, why it matters for electrical systems, and what to check before your next inspection
nfpa_p1: If you're involved in planning, building, or maintaining a hospital in Saudi Arabia, you've likely come across NFPA 99 — the "Health Care Facilities Code" published by the U.S. National Fire Protection Association. It isn't a Saudi legal requirement in the way SASO or Saudi Civil Defense codes are, but it's widely referenced by hospital accreditation bodies, international design consultants, and medical equipment manufacturers operating in the Kingdom, which makes it a de facto standard for anyone building or upgrading a modern healthcare facility here.
nfpa_p2: NFPA 99 is broad — it covers everything from medical gas systems to laboratory safety. For infrastructure and electrical contractors, the most relevant sections are the ones governing "essential electrical systems" (backup power for life-safety and critical branches) and "wet procedure locations" (operating rooms and similar spaces where conductive liquids and electrical equipment are both present).
nfpa_p3: The code classifies patient care spaces into categories based on the risk to patients if electrical power fails or a fault occurs — a general patient room has different requirements than an operating room, and getting that classification right at the design stage determines what equipment you actually need to install.
nfpa_h2_2: Why Wet Procedure Locations Get Special Treatment
nfpa_p4: In an operating room, a patient's body and surgical equipment can create a low-resistance path to ground through conductive fluids. A standard grounded electrical system will trip a breaker the moment a single fault occurs — which is exactly the wrong behavior when a surgical team is mid-procedure and depends on continuous power to monitors, ventilators, and surgical equipment.
nfpa_p5: This is why NFPA 99 requires an isolated power system for these spaces in most cases: it electrically isolates the circuit from ground so a single fault doesn't interrupt power, while a line isolation monitor immediately alerts staff to the fault so it can be corrected — usually between procedures, not during one.
nfpa_check_1: Confirm which NFPA 99 patient care category applies to each space in your facility — this drives every downstream electrical decision.
nfpa_check_2: Verify isolated power panels are installed and functioning in all wet procedure locations (ORs, and other areas your design consultant flags).
nfpa_check_3: Test line isolation monitors on a defined schedule, not just at commissioning — LIM calibration drifts over time.
nfpa_check_4: Confirm essential electrical system branches (life safety, critical, equipment) are properly segregated and backed by UPS or generator as required.
nfpa_check_5: Keep documentation of testing and maintenance — accreditation reviews and insurance audits will ask for it.
nfpa_h2_4: Where This Gets Practical for Facility Managers
nfpa_p6: Most compliance gaps we encounter aren't from bad initial design — they're from maintenance drift. A line isolation monitor that's never recalibrated, a distribution board that was modified without updating documentation, or an operating room repurposed from a lower-risk space without a corresponding electrical upgrade. Building to NFPA 99 once isn't enough; it needs a maintenance program behind it.

ipp_blog_h1: Why Your Hospital Needs Isolated Power Panels
ipp_blog_subhead: The risk they solve, how they work, and when NFPA 99 requires one
ipp_blog_p1: Ask most hospital administrators what keeps them up at night about facility infrastructure, and power reliability is near the top. But there's a more specific risk that's easy to overlook until you understand it: what happens if a single ground fault occurs in an operating room mid-procedure?
ipp_blog_h2_1: The Problem Ordinary Electrical Systems Have in Operating Rooms
ipp_blog_p2: In a standard grounded electrical system, a ground fault — current unintentionally finding a path to ground — trips a breaker to protect people and equipment. That's the correct behavior almost everywhere in a building. But in an operating room, where a patient and surgical equipment can form part of that path through conductive fluids, an abrupt power cut mid-procedure isn't a safety feature. It's a new hazard.
ipp_blog_p3: This is precisely the scenario isolated power systems are designed to prevent.
ipp_blog_h2_2: How an Isolated Power Panel Actually Works
ipp_blog_p4: An isolated power panel (IPP) uses an isolation transformer to separate the operating room's electrical circuit from the building's grounded system. Neither conductor is directly referenced to ground, so a single fault doesn't create the low-resistance path needed to trip a breaker or interrupt power.
ipp_blog_p5: Instead, a line isolation monitor (LIM) continuously watches both conductors for a developing fault and sounds an alarm the moment one occurs — typically well before it becomes dangerous. The surgical team gets a clear signal that something needs attention, without power being interrupted mid-procedure. The fault is usually corrected between procedures rather than during one.
ipp_blog_h2_3: When Is an IPP Actually Required?
ipp_blog_p6: NFPA 99 requires isolated power systems for "wet procedure locations" — spaces where a patient is likely to come into contact with both electrical equipment and conductive liquid at the same time. In practice, this typically covers:
ipp_blog_scenario_3: Certain critical care and intensive care areas, per facility risk assessment
ipp_blog_scenario_4: Some obstetric delivery rooms, depending on procedure type
ipp_blog_p7: The exact classification depends on your facility's risk assessment and design consultant's determination — not every patient care space needs one, but the spaces that do need one absolutely cannot substitute a standard grounded system instead.
ipp_blog_h2_4: What This Means If You're Planning or Renovating a Facility
ipp_blog_p8: If you're building a new operating suite, converting a space to a higher-risk use, or simply inheriting a facility where you're not confident the existing electrical infrastructure matches current code, the isolated power system is not an area to guess on. It requires equipment properly rated for the application (transformer, line isolation monitor, and branch circuit breakers matched to the panel), correct installation and equipotential grounding, and ongoing testing — a LIM that drifts out of calibration defeats the purpose of having one.

cs_ipp_h1: Isolated Power for a Hospital Operating Theatre Suite
cs_ipp_sub: Bringing a multi-theatre surgical suite in the Eastern Province in line with NFPA 99
cs_ipp_c1: A private hospital in the Eastern Province was expanding its surgical capacity and needed the new operating theatres to satisfy NFPA 99 requirements for wet procedure locations. Their design consultant had classified the theatres as Category 1 spaces, which meant isolated power was required rather than optional.
cs_ipp_c2: The complication was not the new build. It was that several existing theatres in the adjoining wing had been commissioned years earlier, and their line isolation monitors had never been recalibrated. Any accreditation review would have looked at the suite as a whole.
cs_ipp_w1: We began with a survey of the existing suite rather than quoting only the new theatres, so the hospital could see the whole compliance picture before committing to a scope.
cs_ipp_w2: For the new theatres we supplied and installed isolated power panels with integrated line isolation monitors, each feeding a dedicated reference-grounding point and the theatre’s critical branch outlets. Panels were selected for compatibility with the Bender and PG LifeLink equipment already used elsewhere in the facility, so the biomedical team would not be maintaining two different families of hardware.
cs_ipp_w3: For the existing theatres we recalibrated the monitors, corrected documentation that no longer matched the installed distribution, and handed over a testing schedule.
cs_ipp_w4: Installation and commissioning were sequenced around the theatre schedule, working in the gaps between surgical lists rather than requiring the suite to close.
cs_ipp_o1: The new theatres were commissioned with isolated power systems and line isolation monitoring in place, and the existing theatres were brought back to a documented, tested state.
cs_ipp_o2: The hospital now holds a single maintenance schedule covering every theatre in the suite. In our experience the majority of NFPA 99 gaps are not design failures but maintenance drift, so the schedule matters as much as the hardware.
cs_ev_h1: EV Charging Rollout Across a Commercial Retail Complex
cs_ev_sub: AC and DC charging for a mixed retail and office development, sized for growth
cs_ev_c1: The operator of a mixed retail and office development wanted EV charging in its parking structure. The commercial driver was tenant demand and Vision 2030 alignment; the constraint was the existing electrical infrastructure.
cs_ev_c2: The initial request was for a large number of fast chargers. An early load assessment showed the incoming supply could not support that without a substation upgrade that would have dominated the budget.
cs_ev_w1: We started with an electrical capacity assessment rather than a charger quotation, because the answer to "how many chargers" is determined by the supply, not by the parking count.
cs_ev_w2: The deployment we recommended mixed a small number of DC fast chargers near the retail entrance, where dwell time is short and speed matters, with a larger number of AC Level 2 units in the office parking area, where vehicles sit for hours and slower charging is sufficient. This served more vehicles per riyal of electrical capacity than an all-DC design.
cs_ev_w3: All units were specified as OCPP-compliant so the operator is not locked to a single vendor’s management platform, and integrated with a payment system so charging could be billed rather than absorbed as a service cost.
cs_ev_w4: Containment and distribution were sized for a second phase, so adding units later means pulling cable, not revisiting the switchgear.
cs_ev_o1: The complex went live with a working mix of AC and DC charging within the existing electrical supply, avoiding the substation upgrade the original brief would have required.
cs_ev_o2: Because the distribution was sized ahead of demand, the operator can expand as EV uptake grows without repeating the civil works.
cs_ups_h1: UPS Replacement on a Healthcare Critical Branch
cs_ups_sub: Replacing end-of-life power backup in a live facility, without a shutdown window
cs_ups_c1: A healthcare facility was running UPS units that had passed end of life. Batteries were no longer holding their rated autonomy, and replacement parts for the units themselves were becoming difficult to source.
cs_ups_c2: The units protected the critical branch feeding patient monitoring and diagnostic equipment. There was no acceptable shutdown window: the equipment they protected could not simply be switched off while the UPS was swapped.

cs_ups_w2: Sizing was based on a measured load survey rather than the nameplate rating of the outgoing units. Critical branches accumulate equipment over years, and the real load rarely matches what was installed against originally.
cs_ups_w3: The changeover was carried out through a temporary bypass arrangement so the protected load stayed energised throughout. Each unit was transferred, commissioned and load-tested before the next was started.
cs_ups_w4: We handed over a battery replacement schedule with the system, since batteries, not electronics, are what typically end a UPS installation’s useful life.
cs_ups_o1: The critical branch is protected by current-generation equipment with full rated autonomy restored and a supported spare parts path.
cs_ups_o2: Clinical operations continued throughout the replacement. No shutdown window was required.

cs_light_c1: A high-rise development required aviation obstruction lighting to mark the structure, plus lighting for a rooftop helipad intended for emergency medical access.

cs_light_w1: We specified obstruction lighting to the intensity class appropriate to the structure’s height, with the fixture layout set by the building’s profile so the outline is marked correctly from every approach angle.

cs_light_w4: Circuits were backed so that a loss of normal supply does not extinguish the obstruction lighting.
cs_light_o1: The structure is marked in line with aviation requirements, and the helipad is lit for night operations.
cs_light_o2: Because failures are monitored and alarmed, the facilities team learns about a failed fixture when it happens rather than at an inspection.

post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_lea: Every isolated power panel in an operating theatre has a line isolation monitor on the front of it, and in most hospitals it is the least understood device in the room. Staff know that green is good and red is bad. Beyond that, the LIM tends to be ignored until an inspector asks for its test records, or until it alarms mid-procedure and nobody in the room is sure whether to stop. NFPA 99 is specific about what this device has to do, and the numbers are worth knowing before either of those happens.
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_h2_: What the Monitor Is Actually Measuring
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_s1_: A line isolation monitor does not measure current flowing through a patient, and it does not detect that a fault has occurred. It continuously measures how well the isolated circuit is still isolated from ground, expressed as the current that would flow if someone completed a path from either isolated conductor to ground.

NFPA 99 calls this the total hazard current, and it has two parts. The fault hazard current is the leakage contributed by everything connected to the isolated system: the cabling, the panel, and every piece of equipment plugged into a receptacle. The monitor hazard current is the leakage contributed by the LIM itself, because the act of measuring requires its own small connection to ground. The figure on the meter is the sum of the two.

That distinction matters the moment you start troubleshooting. A monitor reading 3 mA with nothing plugged in is telling you about the installation itself, which usually means long cable runs and accumulated capacitive leakage. The same monitor reading 3 mA with a fully equipped theatre connected is telling you something completely different, and the fix is not the same.
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_h2_: The Two Numbers That Matter: 5.0 mA and 3.7 mA
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_s2_: NFPA 99 requires the monitor to energise a red signal lamp and an audible warning signal when the total hazard current from either isolated conductor to ground reaches a threshold of 5.0 mA under normal line voltage conditions. That is the alarm point, and it is not something to be adjusted upward because a panel has become a nuisance.

The standard also sets a floor: the line isolation monitor shall not alarm for a fault hazard current of less than 3.7 mA. That second number exists to stop over-sensitive monitors crying wolf. A LIM that alarms at 2 mA is not a more cautious LIM, it is a non-compliant one, and its real effect is to train staff to treat the red lamp as background noise.

NFPA 99 also requires an ammeter indicating the total hazard current, mounted in a plainly visible place on the monitor, with the alarm-on zone at 5.0 mA sitting at approximately the centre of the scale. That layout is deliberate. It lets someone see at a glance how much margin is left, rather than only whether the threshold has already been crossed. If your panel offers a bare red lamp and no meter, it is worth asking when it was last assessed against a current edition of the code.
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_h2_: A Red Lamp Is Not a Power Failure
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_s3_: This is the single most useful thing to teach theatre staff. When the LIM alarms, power has not been interrupted and is not about to be. The alarm means the isolation that protects against a second fault has degraded. The system is still doing exactly what it was installed to do; what it has lost is its safety margin.

The correct response is not to evacuate the theatre or shut the panel down. It is to work out what changed. In practice that means disconnecting recently introduced equipment one item at a time while watching the meter, because the culprit is almost always the last thing wheeled into the room. If the reading does not fall as equipment comes off, the problem is in the fixed wiring and needs an electrician rather than a nurse.

Finishing the procedure and investigating afterwards is a legitimate decision, and it is the one the design intent of NFPA 99 supports. What is not legitimate is silencing the alarm and moving on, because the fault the monitor is reporting is the one that makes the next fault an actual power interruption.
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_h2_: The Test Button, and the Test It Does Not Replace
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_s4_: Every LIM has a test switch that momentarily places a known fault on the isolated system so that the lamp and the audible alarm operate. Pressing it proves the annunciation works. It does not prove the monitor is measuring accurately, because the test circuit is internal and sits well above the threshold being verified.

Calibration drift is the failure mode that actually matters, and it is invisible to the button. A monitor that has drifted to the point where it alarms at 8 mA still passes the button test perfectly: the lamp lights, the buzzer sounds, the log gets signed, and the panel has quietly stopped providing the protection it was installed for. Establishing the real threshold means injecting a calibrated current and reading the response, which is a service task rather than a walk-round task.

Run both, and keep the records separate. The button test is quick enough to do routinely and it catches dead lamps and failed buzzers. The instrumented test catches the drift. Accreditation reviews and insurers ask for evidence of the second one, and a log full of button tests does not answer the question they are asking.
post_nfpa_99_line_isolation_monitors_s5_: Nearly every LIM problem we are called to in the Eastern Province falls into one of three groups. The first is accumulated leakage. A theatre has circuits added over the years, each contributing a little capacitive leakage, until the resting reading sits close enough to 5.0 mA that any ordinary equipment change tips it over. Nothing is faulty. The room has simply outgrown its isolation transformer, and the answer is a load review rather than a new monitor.

The second is damaged flexible cords. A trolley wheel run over the same cable in the same place for two years eventually compromises the insulation, and the resulting leakage appears on the monitor long before it becomes anything a user would notice. That early warning is precisely what the system exists to provide, which is why a rising baseline deserves investigation rather than acceptance.

The third is documentation. A panel gets modified, a circuit is re-fed from somewhere else, and the panel schedule is never updated. Two years later the reading is high and nobody can say with confidence what is connected to the isolated system, so tracing starts from nothing. Keeping the schedule current costs almost nothing and routinely saves a full day on site.

post_sizing_ups_hospital_critical_branch: Ask three consultants to size a UPS for a hospital critical branch and you will get three different answers, usually because they are quietly answering three different questions. The kVA figure is the easy part. What decides whether the installation is still adequate in five years is a set of assumptions that rarely get written down anywhere, and almost never get revisited.
The Critical Branch Is Not the Whole Hospital

NFPA 99 divides a hospital essential electrical system into three branches, and they do not have the same requirements. The life safety branch covers egress lighting, alarm and alerting systems, emergency communications, generator set lighting and elevator control. The critical branch covers the areas and receptacles associated with maintaining patient treatment. The equipment branch feeds the large plant that patient care depends on but that can tolerate a delay, including central suction, medical-surgical vacuum and the large HVAC serving operating rooms.

Getting this split right is the first sizing decision, and it is made on a drawing rather than in a spreadsheet. A UPS sized against a load schedule that has quietly included equipment-branch plant will be substantially oversized and correspondingly expensive. One sized against a schedule that has left out critical-branch receptacles will be undersized in a way that only shows up during an actual outage.

It is worth saying plainly that the UPS does not replace the generator. The generator carries the outage. The UPS carries the seconds the generator cannot, and it conditions the supply for equipment that will not tolerate the transfer itself.
The 10 Seconds That Set the Floor

Hospital generators are required to restore power to the life safety and critical branches within 10 seconds of losing the utility. That is a demanding window: the system has to detect the outage, crank and start the engine, bring it to rated speed and voltage, and complete the automatic transfer, all inside those 10 seconds.

The naive conclusion is that a UPS with 10 seconds of runtime therefore covers the gap. It does not, and sizing to it is the most common mistake we are asked to correct. Ten seconds is the value the code can hold a generator to under test conditions. It is not a value that survives the case the code cannot legislate for, which is the generator that does not start at all, or starts and then trips on its first block load.

A defensible number for the critical branch is normally somewhere between ten and thirty minutes, and the range matters less than the reasoning. That is long enough for a second start attempt, for a manual transfer to an alternate source, or for a controlled wind-down of whatever procedure is under way. Whatever figure is chosen should be a written decision with a rationale attached, because it is the assumption most likely to be challenged after an incident.
Size in kW, Not kVA Alone

A UPS nameplate carries a kVA rating; the load draws kW. The ratio between them is the power factor, and comparing two quotations on kVA alone compares almost nothing. Older UPS designs were commonly rated at 0.8 power factor, so a 100 kVA unit delivered 80 kW. Many modern units are rated at unity, so a 100 kVA unit delivers 100 kW. Those are not the same machine, and they are not the same price.

On the load side, resist the temptation to add up nameplates. A nameplate is a worst-case figure that assumes the device is doing the most demanding thing it can do, and a ward full of equipment never does that simultaneously. Summing nameplates typically produces a number 40 to 60 percent above anything the branch will actually draw, and hospitals pay for that difference twice: once in capital cost, and again in a UPS running at low load where it is least efficient.

The honest method is to measure. Clamp the existing branch over a full working week, capture the peak rather than the average, and then apply headroom as a deliberate decision on top of a measured figure. Where the branch does not exist yet, build the load schedule from the equipment list and apply a diversity factor you are willing to defend, then measure at commissioning and record the result for the next upgrade.
Leave Room for the Load You Have Not Bought Yet

Hospitals grow into their electrical infrastructure faster than almost any other building type. An imaging suite is added, monitoring is upgraded from one device per bed to three, infusion pumps multiply, and a UPS that was sized precisely against a validated load schedule is at capacity in year three. The schedule was not wrong. It was a snapshot.

We normally recommend sizing with 25 to 30 percent headroom above the measured peak, and then checking that the rest of the installation can actually use it. A UPS with spare capacity feeding a distribution board with no spare ways is not spare capacity; it is a number on a nameplate. The same applies to cable sizing and to the room the batteries live in.

Where the budget allows it, a modular UPS architecture converts this from a forecasting problem into a purchasing one. Power modules are added to the frame as the load grows, so the initial spend is matched to the initial load and the capacity arrives when it is needed. The frame has to be specified for the eventual load from the start, which is where the forecasting reappears, but the consequence of getting it wrong is far smaller.
Runtime Is a Battery Decision

It is worth separating the two questions that get conflated in most conversations. The UPS module determines how much power can be supported. The battery string determines how long. Doubling runtime does not require a larger UPS, it requires more battery, and the constraint is usually floor space and floor loading rather than the electronics.

Battery sizing has to be done at end-of-life capacity, not at the capacity of a new string. A battery is generally considered to have reached end of life at 80 percent of rated capacity, and a system that only meets its runtime target on a brand-new string is a system that misses it for most of its service life. The same calculation has to use the temperature the batteries will actually live at, not the 25 degrees the datasheet assumes.

That temperature point is where most hospital UPS installations in this region quietly fail, and it deserves more attention than it usually gets during design. It is also the subject of a separate article, because the arithmetic behind it explains almost every early battery replacement we are called out to.

post_saso_requirements_ev_chargers_saudi: Electric vehicle charging in the Kingdom is governed by a Saudi-modified version of an international standard, and the modifications are the part that matters. A charger that is entirely legal in Europe or East Asia can be non-compliant here, and the difference is not obvious from a product datasheet. In practice most buyers discover it at customs, or when a facility manager asks for documentation that was never going to exist.
The Standard That Actually Applies

The governing document for conductive charging systems is the Saudi amendment SASO IEC 61851-1:2018/AMD1:2022, which adopts the international standard IEC 61851-1 and then varies it to take account of conditions in the Kingdom. Reading the IEC standard alone is not enough, because it is precisely the amendment that removes options the international text permits. Confirm the current revision with SASO or your certification body before you specify against it.

This is a general pattern with SASO adoptions and it is worth internalising before specifying anything. The base standard is international and familiar; the Saudi layer on top narrows it. Suppliers quoting compliance with IEC 61851-1 are not making a false claim, but they are also not answering the question, and the distinction is one a purchaser has to enforce.

Ambient conditions are part of the reason for the narrowing. Equipment specified against a temperate-climate assumption behaves differently in a car park in Dammam in August, and the derating that follows is a real design constraint rather than a paperwork exercise.
The Two Restrictions That Catch People Out

IEC 61851-1 defines four charging modes. Mode 1 is a plain connection to a standard socket with no dedicated protection or communication. Mode 2 adds an in-cable control and protection device, which is the familiar portable cable that comes in the boot of the car. Mode 3 is a fixed installed AC charging station with control pilot communication, and Mode 4 is DC charging with an off-board charger.

The Saudi amendment is blunt about both. Mode 1 supply equipment is not permitted in the Kingdom and is not allowed to be imported — not restricted to certain applications, but excluded outright. Mode 2 is prohibited in public areas, and allowed in private areas only under stated conditions: plugs and socket-outlets to SASO IEC 60309, earth leakage protection on the socket-outlet, and a rating of 16 A at 230 V AC single-phase.

The practical consequence for anyone providing charging to the public is that the installation has to be Mode 3 or Mode 4: a fixed station with proper control pilot communication, protective earthing and dedicated circuit protection. Budgeting on the assumption that sockets and cables will do is the single most common way an EV charging project arrives late and over cost.
DC Fast Charging Brings Its Own Standards

Once a project moves to DC fast charging, the applicable set widens. SASO GSO IEC 61851-23 covers DC electric vehicle charging stations themselves, and SASO IEC 61851-24 covers the digital communication between the DC station and the vehicle that controls the charging process.

Electromagnetic compatibility is handled separately again, and in two parts that are easy to confuse. SASO IEC 61851-21-1 addresses the EMC requirements for the vehicle's on-board charger, while SASO IEC 61851-21-2 covers EMC for off-board charging systems. For a site owner the second is the relevant one, and it is a routine gap in documentation packages assembled by suppliers who mostly sell into other markets.

None of this is exotic for a manufacturer that already sells into regulated markets. The problem is almost never that compliant equipment does not exist; it is that the specific certificates covering the specific model being shipped were never requested at the point of order, and obtaining them retrospectively is slow.
The Certificate of Conformity Is Not Optional

Every EV charger placed on the Saudi market requires a SASO Certificate of Conformity. This is a shipment-level document tied to the product and the consignment, and without it a container does not clear customs. It is not satisfied by a CE mark, a manufacturer declaration or a test report from an unrecognised laboratory.

The commercial risk here sits with whoever bought the equipment, not with whoever made it. A supplier quoting an attractive unit price and leaving conformity as the buyer's problem has transferred a real cost and a real schedule risk without it ever appearing on the quotation. The correct time to ask which certificates will accompany the shipment is before the order is placed, and the correct answer names the standards and the certifying body.

Grid connection is a separate approval from product conformity, and it is worth tracking separately. A charger that is fully certified can still be waiting on the utility, and on projects of any size that permission tends to sit on the critical path rather than beside it.
What This Means Before You Buy

For any charging provision open to the public, start from Mode 3 for AC and Mode 4 for DC, and treat anything cheaper as out of scope rather than as a saving to be evaluated. That single decision removes most of the compliance risk from a project before the electrical design begins.

Ask each shortlisted supplier to name the certificates that will accompany the shipment, for the exact model being quoted, and to state which apply to off-board EMC. A supplier who can answer that in writing without hesitation is a supplier who has shipped here before, and that is worth more than a small difference in unit price.

Finally, specify for the site rather than for the catalogue. Ambient temperature, direct sun on the enclosure, dust ingress, cable management in a busy car park and the physical protection of the unit against vehicle impact all determine whether the installation still works in year three. Compliance gets the equipment into the country; the site conditions decide whether it survives.

post_why_ups_batteries_die_early_saudi_h: A hospital or a data room buys a UPS, the batteries are described as ten-year units, and they are replaced in year three. The usual reaction is that somebody was sold the wrong product. Usually nobody was. The ten-year figure is real, it is simply quoted at a temperature the battery has never once experienced, and the arithmetic connecting the two is not complicated.
The Rule That Explains Almost Every Early Failure

Valve-regulated lead-acid battery life is governed by chemistry, and chemical reaction rates rise with temperature. The relationship follows the Arrhenius equation, and the working rule the manufacturers themselves publish is straightforward: for every 10°C of sustained operating temperature above 25°C, expected battery life is cut roughly in half.

Applied to real numbers this stops being an academic point. A string rated for a given service life at 25°C and operated continuously at 35°C reaches end of life in about half that time. Push the sustained temperature further and the halving applies again. Some manufacturers publish a more aggressive figure of roughly 8°C per halving, which makes the outcome worse rather than better.

There is no maintenance regime that defeats this, and no brand that is exempt from it. Temperature is not one factor among many affecting battery life in this climate; for a system that is otherwise correctly installed and float-charged, it is the dominant one.
The Cabinet Is Hotter Than the Room

The temperature that matters is the temperature at the battery, and that is not the temperature on the wall thermostat. A UPS cabinet typically runs several degrees warmer than the room around it, because the electronics and the batteries are both dissipating heat inside an enclosure designed primarily to keep fingers out.

That gap turns a comfortable-sounding room into a hostile one. A plant room held at 28°C, which few facility managers would consider a problem, can present the cells inside the cabinet with 33°C. Against a 25°C reference that is most of a halving before anything has gone wrong, and it is invisible to anyone checking the room rather than the equipment.

This is also why battery temperature monitoring earns its cost quickly. A logged cell temperature is a number that can be argued with, budgeted against, and used to hold a maintenance contractor to a replacement interval. A room thermostat reading is not evidence about the batteries at all.
Design Life Is a Laboratory Number

The phrase to be careful with in any quotation is design life. It is a float-service figure obtained under controlled conditions, at 25°C, with a correctly regulated charging voltage and without meaningful discharge cycling. It describes what the product is capable of, not what a given installation will get from it.

Two things routinely erode it further, independent of ambient heat. The first is cycling: a site with frequent short outages works its batteries in a way float-service testing does not represent. The second is charging voltage that is not temperature-compensated, which pushes a hot battery further into the accelerated ageing it is already experiencing.

None of this makes design life a dishonest number, and it is still the right basis for comparing two products against each other. It is simply the wrong basis for planning a replacement budget, and treating it as a schedule is how facilities end up funding an unplanned replacement out of an operating budget that had nothing set aside for it.
What Actually Fixes It

The first and largest intervention is to cool the batteries specifically, rather than the room generally. Where the installation allows it, batteries belong in their own cabinet or their own room, held near 25°C and cooled independently of the equipment that shares the space. That single change is worth more than any other item on this list, and it is the one most often value-engineered out at design stage.

Second, insist on temperature-compensated charging. A charger that reduces float voltage as battery temperature rises stops the charging regime from compounding the damage the ambient conditions are already doing. It is a configuration option on most modern UPS systems and it is frequently left at its default.

Third, monitor and log. Cell or string temperature, float voltage and periodic impedance readings turn battery replacement from an emergency into a scheduled item. The goal is not to prevent ageing, which is not available, but to know accurately where the string is in its life so the replacement is planned, budgeted and carried out on a normal working day.
Knowing When to Replace

A battery is conventionally considered to have reached end of life when it can no longer deliver 80 percent of its rated capacity. That threshold matters because the decline is not linear: performance holds up reasonably well and then falls away quickly, so a string that tests marginally today is not a string with months of comfortable margin left.

Impedance testing is the practical monitoring tool, because it can be done without discharging the system and it identifies individual weak cells rather than an average. A single failing cell degrades an entire string, and finding it early is the difference between replacing one block and replacing everything. A full capacity discharge test is more definitive and should be part of the schedule, but it is an event rather than a routine.

The failure mode worth avoiding is the one where the batteries are tested for the first time by an actual outage. The system reports healthy, the utility fails, and the string delivers a fraction of its rated runtime. Everything in this article exists to make sure that is not the moment anyone finds out.

lead_what_heading: What Is Lead Sheet Radiation Shielding?
lead_what_p1: Lead sheet shielding is sheet lead — or lead-lined panels — built into the walls, doors, and viewing windows of rooms where X-ray, CT, fluoroscopy, or radiotherapy equipment is used. Because lead attenuates ionizing radiation efficiently at a manageable thickness, it lets a room stay a normal size while keeping radiation exposure outside the room within regulated limits.
lead_what_p2: The required thickness is not a standard number applied everywhere — it is calculated per room from the equipment's beam energy, how often it is used, how close adjacent occupied spaces are, and how those spaces are used. Get the calculation wrong and a room is either under-protected or shielded far beyond what it needs, at needless cost.
